title: Model-stage Quantization Fallbacks and Bounded Degradation Orchestration - PRD (draft)
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a Dedicated-capacity feature that orchestrates graceful, bounded-quality degradation during capacity pressure by (1) progressively switching served model variants across a model-stage ladder (fp32 -> int8/4-bit quantized -> distilled variant) and (2) combining that with per-tenant degradation budgets, regional affinity controls, and ephemeral compute tagging for stronger isolation. The goal is to keep request latency and availability within SLOs while preserving best-effort output quality where possible, and to offer operators predictable economics and auditability when degradation occurs.

Why this problem matters:
- Dedicated customers expect predictable latency and capacity guarantees. Under sudden demand spikes or partial pool failure we currently either throttle traffic or failover to different pools, both of which can cause higher latency or user-visible errors.
- Pure throttling or hard preemption leads to revenue loss for customers and bad UX.
- Quantization/approx model variants exist but switching is often all-or-nothing and lacks governance: who gets degraded, by how much, for how long, and how to measure impact?

Design goals (what success looks like):
1) Bounded quality regressions: any automatic degradation must be constrained by tenant-specific budgets and global policies. Customers can opt into or out of automated degradation.
2) Latency-first behavior: preserve per-request latency SLOs. Degradation is only triggered when latency headroom is at risk or capacity pool is unavailable.
3) Auditability + observability: every switch must be logged with reasons (capacity event id, trigger signals), and quality regressions must be measurable against golden prompt sets.
4) Per-tenant fairness and isolation: avoid noisy-neighbor quality erosion by mixing per-tenant budgets with ephemeral compute tagging and placement hints.
5) Developer controls: expose simple policy knobs and API headers so customers can indicate preference (latency | quality | cost) per request or per route.

Non-goals:
- This is not an attempt to replace long-term provisioning commitments or billing model. It’s an availability/fidelity orchestration layer to reduce customer-visible disruption.
- We will not auto-train or modify models at runtime. Only variant selection and routing is in-scope.

Feature components (user-facing):
A) Degradation Policy object (per-dedicated-tenant config):
  - enabled: boolean
  - budget_minutes_per_week: integer (how many minutes of degraded service allowed)
  - max_stage_drop: integer (how many steps down the model-stage ladder allowed)
  - priority_window: optional list of time ranges when degradation is disallowed (e.g., business hours)
  - route_overrides: map of route -> preference (latency|quality|cost)
  - notification_webhook: URL
  - audit_retention_days: integer

B) Model-stage Ladder and Variant Catalog (platform-managed):
  - Define for each model family a chain of verified variants: exact -> int8 -> 4-bit -> distill-lite
  - Each variant has an SLO-profile (latency percentile at given qps, quality delta on eval prompts, tokens-per-second cost estimate)
  - Certified transition paths (not all models have a distill stage)

C) Autoscale-integrated trigger pipeline:
  - inputs: queue-length, p99 latency, GPU utilization, pool health, per-tenant budget state
  - a rule engine that determines whether to (1) increase replicas, (2) borrow ephemeral compute, (3) activate degradation for a tenant or (4) redirect to fallback pool
  - multi-signal confirmation to avoid flapping (e.g., require p99 latency > threshold for 30s AND GPU saturating)

D) Isolation controls and ephemeral compute tagging:
  - ephemeral compute tags: when serving degraded variants, runtime marks instances as 'degradation-tag:tenant-X' to limit co-location with other tenants in same pool, reducing secondary quality impact
  - soft affinity enforcement: scheduler tries to place 'degradation-tag' instances on nodes with low cross-tenant interference (NUMA, exclusive SM, or spare GPU partitions)
  - tenant-specific isolation lanes: customers with higher tiers can opt to never be scheduled on a degraded node.

E) Observability and eval feedback:
  - persistent per-tenant golden set and periodic eval runs comparing pre/post-fallback outputs (accuracy & hallucination metrics)
  - dashboards: minutes of degradation, count of degraded requests, average delta-to-golden, and cost impact per tenant
  - automated alerting thresholds when avg quality delta exceeds customer-specified tolerance

Operator/Platform behavior (how it works end-to-end):
1) Detection: autoscaler observes a capacity pressure event and flags pool as at-risk for latency SLOs.
2) Candidate selection: rule engine consults tenant policies; picks tenants allowed to be degraded (respecting budget/minutes), sorts by degravation-priority (lowest contract tier first unless policy overrides).
3) Execution: for selected tenants, routing layer swaps model endpoint variant to next ladder stage for a controlled fraction of traffic (canary style: 10% -> 50% -> 100%) with fast rollback hooks.
4) Isolation: scheduler tags any newly provisioned degraded containers with ephemeral tags and attempts preferred placement.
5) Monitoring: continuous evals run on a sampled subset of degraded requests. Automated rollback if quality delta or hallucination rate exceeds thresholds.

APIs and control-plane:
- PUT /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/degradation_policy  (body = Degradation Policy object)
- GET  /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/degradation_state
- POST /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/golden_eval_run  (kicks immediate eval)
- Request header hints: X-Redwood-Pref: latency|quality|cost, X-Redwood-Quality-Threshold: 0.92 (0-1 scale)

SLOs and metrics to track:
- Safety: <= 1% of requests experience degraded variants outside configured budget windows
- Latency: maintain p95 and p99 SLOs even during event by combining degradation and ephemeral compute; measure delta vs baseline
- Quality: mean delta-to-golden <= tenant.threshold during allowed degradation; if breached trigger rollback
- Observability: all degradation events logged with event_id and trace links for postmortem (audit_retention_days applies)

Operational playbooks (examples):
- Burst shortfall (10-30m): prefer ephemeral compute borrow if available; if not, enable 1-stage degradation for <budget window; notify tenant; auto-roll forward if metrics stable.
- Pool-wide partial outage (1-2h): apply staged swapping by tenant priority, enable regional spillover to other pools, and open ticket for capacity replenish.
- Prolonged overload (>2h): degrade only non-critical routes; inject throttling gracefully otherwise and engage sales/CS for customer outreach.

Security & compliance notes:
- Golden eval prompts and eval outputs for customer-owned datasets must reside in tenant-controlled storage when requested (privacy).
- Degradation audit trails are included in compliance exports for customers under enterprise contracts.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (Experiment, 4 weeks): internal-only proof-of-concept on a single pool, manual trigger and smoke dashboards.
- Phase 1 (Alpha, 8 weeks): opt-in customers, limited set of model families and a single quantization path; expose simple per-tenant budget UI in Console.
- Phase 2 (Beta, 12 weeks): widen to more pools, add ephemeral compute tagging logic, integrate canary percentages, automatic rollback.
- Phase 3 (GA): full catalog support, contract-level policies, SLA language for behavior when degradation occurs.

Implementation risks & mitigation:
- Risk: Quality regressions are larger than predicted for some prompts. Mitigation: conservative default budgets, pre-certification of variants on tenant golden sets, and fast rollback hooks.
- Risk: Tags/placement logic increases scheduler complexity. Mitigation: start with soft tagging + best-effort placement and observe scheduling metrics before enforcing strict isolation.
- Risk: Customers may view degradation as a downgrade to SLA. Mitigation: clear opt-in, transparent console notifications, and billing communication if cost tradeoffs are presented.

Open questions:
- How to price/discount minutes-of-degradation? Flat monthly credit, or pay-as-you-go lower-rate? (sales/finance input needed).
- What default golden set should we use for open-model variants to compute delta when customers do not provide their own?
- How to certify a model variant as acceptable for automatic swap (what performance regressions are tolerable)? Define a certification pipeline.

Next steps (owners):
- Prod: Samir Chen - prototype autoscale trigger hook and canary swap logic (2 sprints).
- Applied ML: Lena Ortiz - build evaluation harness to compute delta-to-golden and hallucination signals for candidate variants (3 sprints).
- Console: Jonah Patel - add degradation policy UI and notification surface (2 sprints).
- Solutions Eng / CS: Priya Rao - draft customer-facing docs and opt-in templates for pilot customers (1 sprint).

Notes / raw brainstorms (informal):
- Could combine with Dedicated billing windows: e.g., customers accept graded quality to save 10% on monthly commitments; show simulation of expected quality minutes per month.
- Consider a second ladder axis: instead of only quantization/distill, could also swap to smaller context window variants or instruction-tuned vs base models depending on route semantics.
- We must check our telemetry cost — running continuous golden evals at scale is expensive; consider sampling strategies.

Appendix: simple event example (timeline)
- 14:05 pool p-np2 reports p99 latency spike > 2x baseline, p99 sustained for 45s
- 14:06 rule engine evaluates and finds ephemeral compute pool empty; 14:06-14:08 select tenants A/B/C eligible (respect budget)
- 14:08 swap A to int8 for 10% traffic as canary; metrics show latency improvement; eval run on sampled 50 responses; delta within threshold
- 14:10 increase to 50% traffic; 14:12 stable -> 100% swap for tenant A; schedule tags applied
- 14:20 apply similar for tenant B; tenant C opts out -> traffic routed to fallback in another region
- 15:05 pool recovers; automated rollback triggered and audit log created

---
This document is intentionally rough — a functional spec to discuss architecture tradeoffs and pilot plan. Pull requests/ideas welcome in the runtime repo and the linear ticket in linked_artifacts.
